lead: This unit is about turning requirements into a design: the parts of a system, how they fit together, and how to draw them. After it you can split a system into modules, choose an architecture and a set of patterns, sketch a user interface, and read and draw the main UML diagrams.
about: Unit 3 starts where requirements end. Chapter 3.1 gives the design process and the quality attributes a design must protect. Chapter 3.2 supplies the working tools: abstraction, modularity, functional decomposition, cohesion and coupling. Chapter 3.3 lifts modules into an architecture and compares layered, client-server and pipe-filter styles. Chapter 3.4 adds reusable design patterns: MVC, observer, adapter and facade. Chapter 3.5 covers user interface design and its three golden rules. The last three chapters are notation: 3.6 class diagrams for static structure, 3.7 sequence and collaboration diagrams for message order, and 3.8 state, activity, component and deployment diagrams. Every formula and diagram is small enough to hold in your head the night before the exam.

chapters.idea: Design turns a requirements model into a design model — data, architecture, interfaces, components, deployment — and every choice is judged against quality attributes.
chapters.depth: Where design sits in the life cycle, and the design process: requirements model in, design model out. Quality guidelines and attributes: maintainability, dependability, security, efficiency, acceptability; some syllabi use ISO 25010 names, some use McCall's factors, so learn the idea and give three or four names with a one-line meaning each. The evolution of design: modular, then object-oriented, then pattern-based and aspect-oriented. The five elements of the design model, one short paragraph each. Keep every attribute to one line and show one trade-off pair; no measurement formulas here.

figure.title: The design model
figure.aria: The design model fans out into five design elements, with architectural design picked out because the next chapter builds on it.

chapters.example: A ticket-booking site must be available 99.9 % of the year and must carry 40,000 users in the 10 a.m. booking window. (a) Name the two quality attributes. (b) How much downtime does 99.9 % allow in a 365-day year? (c) Give one design decision for each. Answer: (a) reliability (availability) and performance (scalability). (b) 0.001 × 365 × 24 h = 8.76 h, about 8 h 46 min a year. (c) Availability: run two copies of the booking service behind a load balancer, so one server can fail. Performance: keep the seat map in a cache and hold the seat lock in memory, so the database is not hit on every page view.
chapters.trap: Writing quality attributes as a wish list with no trade-off. A full answer names the attribute, the design decision that buys it, and the attribute it costs — encrypting card data buys security and costs response time.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 (process models) and Unit 2 (functional and non-functional requirements).
chapters.leave: Cohesion and coupling measures to 3.2, architecture styles to 3.3, testability measures to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A design is good when each module hides its own information, does one job (high cohesion), and leans lightly on other modules (low coupling).
chapters.depth: Abstraction (procedural and data), problem partitioning, functional decomposition, stepwise refinement, separation of concerns, information hiding, modularity and its cost. Functional independence = cohesion + coupling: name the seven cohesion levels from coincidental to functional and the coupling levels from content to data, worst to best, with an example of the worst and the best. Object-oriented design concepts: class, object, inheritance, encapsulation, polymorphism; design classes that are complete, sufficient, primitive and cohesive. One short paragraph each on refactoring and on aspects.

figure.aria: A payroll system is split level by level into four functions, and the deductions function is broken again into three parts, showing functional decomposition.

chapters.example: One class, Billing, does four jobs: it computes GST, prints a thermal receipt, writes a row into MySQL, and sends an SMS. (a) What is the cohesion of Billing? (b) Split it and name the coupling you get. Answer: (a) coincidental cohesion, the worst level — the four jobs share no data and are tied only by living in one class. (b) Four classes: GstCalculator, ReceiptPrinter, BillRepository, SmsNotifier, with Billing kept as a controller that calls all four. Billing → GstCalculator passes one amount in rupees and gets the tax back, which is data coupling, the best kind. Billing → BillRepository passes the whole Bill object, which is stamp coupling; fix it by passing a small Bill DTO instead.
chapters.trap: Getting the directions backwards: high cohesion is good, high coupling is bad. Marks are also lost for saying functional decomposition and modularity are the same thing — decomposition is the act of splitting, modularity is the property of the result.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 (the design model) and Unit 2 (class-based requirements models).
chapters.leave: Architecture styles to 3.3, pattern catalogues to 3.4, class-diagram notation to 3.6, refactoring as maintenance work to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Architecture is the set of big early decisions about a system's parts, and a style is a named template for making those decisions.
chapters.depth: What software architecture is and why it is fixed early. The architectural design steps: take structural elements from the requirements, group them into subsystems, map them onto a style, check them against the quality attributes. Styles in detail: layered and n-tier (with the layer-versus-tier distinction), client-server, pipe-filter. Name repository/blackboard and event-driven styles in one line each. For each of the three main styles give structure, one attribute it helps, one it hurts, and one place it is used. One paragraph on data design (tables, keys, normalisation). Close with a case study of a booking system mapped onto a 3-tier design, because many syllabi ask a case study here.

figure.aria: Four layers stacked from the user side down to the data side, with the business logic layer picked out as the one carrying the rules.

chapters.example: A log pipeline has three filters: parse takes 4 ms per record, validate takes 6 ms, format takes 2 ms. Records arrive at 100 per second. (a) What is the steady-state throughput of the pipeline? (b) What is the latency of one record? (c) Where is the bottleneck, and what does a second copy of that filter buy? Answer: (a) the slowest stage sets the rate, 1 ÷ 0.006 s ≈ 166.7 records per second, which is above the 100 per second arriving, so the pipeline keeps up. (b) latency = 4 + 6 + 2 = 12 ms. (c) validate is the bottleneck; two copies working in parallel give 2 ÷ 0.006 s ≈ 333 records per second.
chapters.trap: Treating layer and tier as synonyms. A layer is a logical group of code; a tier is a physical place where code runs. A 3-layer design can be deployed as 2 tiers when business logic and data access share a server.
chapters.leave: MVC and the GoF patterns to 3.4, component and deployment notation to 3.8, deployment automation to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A pattern is a named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem, and it is worth using when its cost is smaller than the problem it removes.
chapters.depth: Why patterns exist. The GoF grouping into creational, structural and behavioural patterns, one line on each with two example names beyond the four studied. Then the four named patterns, each with intent, structure, when to use it and what it costs: MVC (model, view, controller; some syllabi call it an architectural pattern), observer (subject and observers, one-to-many, push versus pull), adapter (object adapter versus class adapter, converts one interface into another), facade (one simple interface over many subsystems; it adds no new function). Describe structure with role names only; full class notation waits for 3.6.

figure.aria: Two observers register with the subject and each is then notified and pulls the new state back, which is the observer pattern in message order.

chapters.example: Pick a pattern for each case and say why. (a) A stock-price feed has 500 registered clients and must push every price change to all of them. (b) A new app must call an old bank API whose methods are named debitAcct(...) and take the amount as an int in paise. (c) A dashboard screen has 30 subsystems behind it and the screen code should call one method per panel. Answer: (a) observer — at 20 price changes per second and 500 clients, pushing gives 20 × 500 = 10,000 update messages per second and no polling; polling all 500 clients every 100 ms would cost 5,000 requests per second even when nothing changes. (b) adapter — it converts the call and the rupees to paise (₹1 = 100 paise) without touching the old code. (c) facade — one DashboardFacade with methods such as loadSalesPanel() hides the 30 subsystems.
chapters.trap: Adapter versus facade. An adapter changes an interface into the one the client already expects, and wraps one mismatched class. A facade puts a new, simpler interface in front of many classes. If the answer says 'wraps many classes to make them easy', it is a facade.
chapters.prereq: 3.2 (abstraction, information hiding) and 3.3 (architecture, where MVC usually appears).
chapters.leave: Class diagram notation to 3.6, sequence notation to 3.7, pattern-based testing to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A user interface is designed by analysing users, tasks, content and environment, then applying three golden rules: put the user in control, reduce memory load, make the interface consistent.
chapters.depth: Why the interface is most of what the user sees of quality. The three golden rules with two concrete design moves each. Interface analysis: user analysis, task analysis, content and display analysis, work-environment analysis. The design steps and evaluation through prototypes and refinement. Modern GUI elements: menus (menu bar, pull-down, context menu), windows, icons, buttons, panels, scroll bars, error messages — what each is for and one rule for using it. Error messages: plain language, say what happened, say what to do next, no bare codes. One short paragraph on accessibility: font size, colour contrast, keyboard-only operation.

figure.title: Interface design steps
figure.aria: Four analysis steps feed the interface design, which is then evaluated and sent back for refinement.

chapters.example: An electricity-bill payment screen asks for the consumer number (12 digits), the amount typed twice, and a bill ID the user must copy from an SMS received that morning. (a) Count the memory items and name the golden rule that is broken. (b) Redesign it and count the fields removed. Answer: (a) three memory items — the 12-digit consumer number, the amount retyped, the bill ID from the SMS. 'Reduce the user's memory load' is broken, and so is 'place the user in control', because the user cannot see the bill before paying. (b) Let the consumer number fetch the bill, show the amount as read-only text, and drop the second amount entry: 3 fields become 1 and the memory items fall from 3 to 1.
chapters.trap: Answering with 'make it attractive and simple'. Marks come from naming the analysis step (user, task, content, environment), the golden rule, and one concrete control — a drop-down instead of a free text field, a read-only amount, an error message that says what to do.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 (use cases give the tasks) and 3.1 (usability as a quality attribute).
chapters.leave: Usability and accessibility testing to Unit 4; web and mobile layout patterns to Unit 4's application testing.

chapters.idea: A class diagram is the static picture of a system: the classes, their attributes and operations, and the relationships between them.
chapters.depth: The UML conceptual model in one line each: things, relationships, diagrams. Class notation: three compartments, visibility marks + − # ~, underlined static members, abstract class and interface names italic or marked <<interface>>. Relationships: association with role names and multiplicity (1, 0..1, *, 1..*, 2..4), aggregation with the hollow diamond, composition with the filled diamond, generalization with the hollow triangle, dependency with a dashed arrow, realization from a class to an interface. Four steps from a paragraph of requirements to a finished diagram. Object diagrams in two lines.

figure.aria: A customer places many orders, an order is made of order lines, each order line points at one item, and an order may have one payment.

chapters.example: Draw the class diagram for a bank. A customer holds one or more accounts; an account may have two or more holders when it is a joint account; a branch has many accounts; every transaction belongs to exactly one account. (a) How many classes? (b) Give the multiplicity on each of the four lines. Answer: (a) four classes — Customer, Account, Branch, Transaction. (b) Customer 1 .. 0..* Account, and read back Account 2..* .. 1..* Customer because a joint account needs at least two holders (use 1..* if the question does not mention joint accounts). Branch 1 .. 0..* Account. Account 1 .. 0..* Transaction, and Transaction 1..1 Account. Add the filled diamond on Account–Transaction if a transaction cannot exist after its account is closed.
chapters.trap: Putting behaviour on a static diagram. A class diagram never shows time or message order; if your arrows carry a fixed sequence, you have drawn a sequence diagram instead. Second trap: the hollow diamond is aggregation and the filled diamond is composition — a composition part dies with its whole.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 (class-based requirements modelling) and 3.2 (abstraction, classes and objects).
chapters.leave: Message order to 3.7, states and components to 3.8, use case diagrams to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Interaction diagrams show how objects talk over time: sequence diagrams with time running down the page, collaboration diagrams with numbered links.
chapters.depth: What both diagrams share: a set of objects, links, messages, and one scenario each. Sequence diagrams: actor and object lifelines, activation bars, synchronous message (solid line, filled arrowhead), asynchronous message (open arrowhead), return message (dashed), object creation and destruction, frames for loop and alt/else with guard conditions. Collaboration diagrams — some syllabi call them communication diagrams: object boxes, links, and nested numbering 1, 1.1, 1.1.1, 2 … that carries the order without a time axis. Three steps to convert one form into the other. Link both to a use case scenario from Unit 2.

figure.aria: Time runs downward as the user inserts a card, the ATM checks the PIN and then debits the bank, and dashed arrows carry the returns back.

chapters.example: Convert this sequence into a collaboration diagram: the user inserts a card (step 1), the ATM asks the bank to verify the PIN (1.1), the bank replies OK (1.1.1), the user asks for ₹2,000 (2), the ATM debits the bank (2.1), the bank approves (2.1.1), the ATM hands out the cash (2.2). (a) Write the numbering. (b) How many links are there, and how many messages travel on each? Answer: (a) exactly as listed — 1, 1.1, 1.1.1 on the first exchange and 2, 2.1, 2.1.1, 2.2 on the second. (b) two links. User–ATM carries 3 messages (1, 2, 2.2); ATM–Bank carries 4 messages (1.1, 1.1.1, 2.1, 2.1.1).
chapters.trap: Writing message numbers on a sequence diagram, or drawing a time axis on a collaboration diagram. Sequence means time down the page and no numbers; collaboration means numbers on links and no time axis. Also, a return is a dashed arrow, not a new call.
chapters.prereq: 3.6 (the objects come from the classes) and Unit 2 (use cases supply the scenarios).
chapters.leave: Class structure and multiplicities to 3.6; state and activity diagrams to 3.8.

chapters.idea: Each remaining UML diagram answers one question: state chart — how one object changes over its life; activity — the order of actions in a workflow; component — how software parts plug together; deployment — which hardware runs what.
chapters.depth: State chart: states, initial (filled circle) and final (bullseye) states, transitions written event [guard] / action, composite and nested states, and when to use it. Activity: initial node, action, decision and merge diamonds, fork and join bars, swimlanes, and when to use it. Component: components, provided and required interfaces (ball and socket), ports, and when to use it. Deployment: nodes, artifacts inside nodes, communication paths with their protocol, and when to use it. Give one line on when not to use each diagram, because exams ask you to choose.

figure.aria: One order object moves forward through four events along the top, and three dashed cancel transitions drop into the cancelled state.

chapters.example: A food-delivery order moves Placed → Accepted → Preparing → Out for delivery → Delivered, and may be cancelled from any step before Out for delivery. (a) How many states and how many transitions does the state chart have? (b) Which guard blocks a late cancellation? Answer: (a) five states on the main path, plus one Cancelled state and a final state; transitions are the 4 forward ones plus 3 cancel ones = 7. (b) a cancel event is accepted only when the state is Placed, Accepted or Preparing, so the guard reads [state ≠ Out for delivery]; once payment is captured the guard also carries [payment not captured].
chapters.trap: Using an activity diagram for the states of one object, or a state chart for a workflow shared by many actors. Rule of thumb: many objects and one flow is an activity diagram; one object and many events is a state chart. Second trap: putting software classes on a deployment diagram — nodes are hardware or execution environments, and components appear inside them only as deployed artifacts.
chapters.prereq: 3.6 and 3.7 (notation and object thinking); Unit 2 use cases give the scenario.
chapters.leave: Use case diagrams to Unit 2; building test cases from state machines to Unit 4.
